'''Maurice W. Long''' (April 20, 1925 – October 14, 2023) was an American [[electrical engineer]], radar engineer, and physicist. He served as director of the [[Georgia Tech Research Institute]] from 1968 to 1975.<ref name="makers">{{cite web|url=http://www.gtri.gatech.edu/gtri75/history-makers|title=History Makers|publisher=[[Georgia Tech Research Institute]]|accessdate=2010-07-08|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100616174329/http://www.gtri.gatech.edu/gtri75/history-makers|archive-date=2010-06-16|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref name="gtri">{{cite web|url=http://www.gtri.gatech.edu/gtri75/history-makers/dr-maurice-w-long|title=Dr. Maurice W. Long|publisher=[[Georgia Tech Research Institute]]|accessdate=2010-07-08|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100619074538/http://www.gtri.gatech.edu/gtri75/history-makers/dr-maurice-w-long|archive-date=2010-06-19|url-status=dead}}</ref> He worked as a part-time radar consultant, principal research engineer at GTRI and adjunct professor of electrical engineering at [[Southern Polytechnic State University]].<ref name="radarcon">{{cite web|url=http://www.radarcon2008.org/tutorial_01.php?menu=3|title=2009 IEEE Radar Conference|publisher=[[IEEE]]|accessdate=2010-07-08|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110727194435/http://www.radarcon2008.org/tutorial_01.php?menu=3|archive-date=2011-07-27|url-status=dead}}</ref>

== Education ==
Long received a [[Bachelor of Science]] in electrical engineering from the [[Georgia Institute of Technology]] in 1946. He also received a [[Master of Science]] in physics and a [[PhD]] from Georgia Tech, and a Master of Science in electrical engineering from the [[University of Kentucky]].<ref name="scitechpub">{{cite web|url=http://www.scitechpublishing.com/index.asp?PageAction=VIEWPROD&ProdID=159|title=Airborne Early Warning System Concepts, Third Edition|publisher=SciTech Publishing|accessdate=2010-07-08}}</ref>

== Career ==
Long began his career at the Engineering Experiment Station (now known as the [[Georgia Tech Research Institute]]) in 1946 as he completed his bachelor's degree in electrical engineering at Georgia Tech.<ref name="ens" /><!-- p400 --> By 1963, he was serving as the chief of the Electronics Division of the Engineering Experiment Station.<ref name="ens" /><!-- p325 --> Long succeeded [[Wyatt Whitley]] as director of the Engineering Experiment Station in 1968 and was also given the title of associate dean for research as part of institute president [[Edwin D. Harrison]]'s attempts to bring the academic departments and the station closer together.<ref name="ens">{{cite book|first=Robert C.|last=McMath|author2=Ronald H. Bayor |author3=James E. Brittain |author4=Lawrence Foster |author5=August W. Giebelhaus |author6=Germaine M. Reed |authorlink=Bob McMath|title=Engineering the New South: Georgia Tech 1885-1985|publisher=[[University of Georgia Press]]|location=Athens, GA}}</ref><!-- p363 --> In 1970, institute president [[Arthur Hansen]] moved to absorb the station entirely into the institute. Long resisted this move, feeling that it would compromise the effectiveness of the station.<ref name="gtri"/><ref name="ens"/><!-- p400 --> The complete integration of the Engineering Experiment Station and the institute's academic units never occurred, in part due to Long's outspokenness on the issue and in part due to [[James E. Boyd (scientist)|James E. Boyd]]'s selection as interim president upon Hansen's resignation in 1971.<ref name="gtri" /><ref name="ens" /><!-- p400 -->

During Long's tenure as director, the Engineering Experiment station set a new record of $5.2 million in grants and contracts in [[fiscal year]] 1970–71 in spite of an economic recession and government budget cuts.<ref name="gtri" /> In July 1971, the station lost half of its state funding, resulting in layoffs of a large number of research personnel and the reorganization of the station to make it more financially independent by shifting its focus toward soliciting revenue-generating contracts.<ref name="ens" /><!-- p401 --> Long's annual report of 1972-73 reflected this change, where he defined the station as "a client-oriented research center supported primarily by Federal and industrial grants."<ref name="ens" /><!-- p401 --> The shift in funding led the station toward more environmentally-related research and the development of alternative energy sources.<ref name="ens" /><!-- p401 -->

Long retired as director of the Engineering Experiment Station in 1975, but continued to serve as a consultant. He also worked as a private radar consultant, most notably serving as a liaison scientist with the [[U.S. Office of Naval Research]] in [[London, England]].<ref name="scitechpub" /> He has written and edited several books on radar systems including ''Radar Reflectivity of Land and Sea'' and ''Airborne Early Warning System Concepts''.<ref name="radarcon" />

==Personal life and death==
Long married [[Beverly Long (activist)|Beverly Benson]] in 1963, the couple had two children together.<ref>{{Cite web| title=EES starts new paper | url=https://history.gtri.gatech.edu/files/media/station-news/SN_1972_10.pdf | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230926014106/https://history.gtri.gatech.edu/files/media/station-news/SN_1972_10.pdf | archive-date=2023-09-26}}</ref>

Long died on October 14, 2023, aged 98.<ref>{{cite web |title=Maurice W. Long |url=https://www.legacy.com/us/obituaries/fbnewsleader/name/maurice-long-obituary?id=53366864 |website=Legacy |access-date=22 October 2023}}</ref>
